Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I teach my friend, a fisherman gone blind, to cast true left, right or center and how far between lily pads and the fallen cedar. Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? Our bait, worms, have no professors, they live in darkness, can be taught fear of light. Cut into threes even sixes they live separate lives, recoil from light. He tells me, “I am seldom blind when I dream, morning is anthracite, I play blind man’s bluff, I cannot find myself, my shoe, the sink, tell time, but that’s spilled milk and ink, the lost and found I cannot find. I can tell the difference between a mollusk and a whelk, a grieving liar and a lemon rind.” Laughing, he says, “I still hope the worm will turn,pink, lank, and warm, dined out on apples of good fortune. Books have a faintly legible smell. Divorced from the sun, I am a kind of bachelor henpecked by the night. Sometimes I use my darkness well— in the overcast and sunlight of my mind. I can still wink, sing, my eyes are songs.” Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last? He could not fish, he could not walk, he fell in his own feces. He wept. He died where he fell.The power of beauty to right all wrongs is hard for me to sell.

Here is a complete rewrite of the text, preserving all original details, facts, and themes while using new vocabulary and phrasing:

***

I instruct a sightless companion—formerly an avid angler—on how to accurately aim his fishing line across all directions, judging the exact gaps between aquatic plants and a submerged cedar tree. One is led to wonder about the value of the void: how much time remains for this gloom? 

Our bait consists of earthworms, creatures lacking any formal education that dwell in total pitch-blackness and can be conditioned to dread brightness. Even if sliced into three or six separate fragments, each piece continues to survive independently, flinching away from illumination. 

My friend confides in me that his vision typically returns when he slumbers, whereas waking up feels like dark coal. In his daily routine, he feels as though he is playing a game of blindfolded tag—unable to locate his physical identity, his footwear, or the washbasin, nor can he tell the hour. Yet he dismisses these troubles as irreversible mishaps beyond recovery. Still, he insists he retains a sharp sensory perception: he can easily distinguish a generic shellfish from a spiral sea snail, or spot a dishonest mourner just as readily as he identifies a piece of citrus peel. 

With a laugh, he mentions holding out hope for a favorable turn of events, picturing a healthy, slender worm nourished by good fortune. He notes that printed literature carries a faint scent that can be mentally deciphered. Cut off from daylight, he likens himself to a single man constantly nagged by the nighttime. Nevertheless, he occasionally harnesses this shadow world to his advantage within the shifting inner climate of his mind. He retains the ability to flutter an eyelid and belt out a tune, viewing his unseeing eyes as a form of music. 

Once more, the thought arises: gloom is a rare treasure, but how long can it endure? 

Eventually, his condition degraded to the point where he could no longer fish or balance on his feet. He collapsed into his own bodily waste, wept, and passed away in the very spot he landed. Because of such a tragic end, I find it impossible to persuade anyone that aesthetic grace holds the power to remedy life's profound suffering.

Here is a complete, narrative expansion of the bullet points:

***

For years, our mornings on the river were governed by a shared geometry. Sitting in the rowboat, I became my friend’s eyes, guiding his casts through a language of precise spatial instructions: *“Two o’clock, fifteen feet out, just beyond the edge of the lily pads.”* He would launch his line with remarkable accuracy, relying on my vocal coordinates to navigate the unseen water. This careful dance of direction and trust turned our fishing trips into an art form, allowing him to feel the rhythm of the river despite the shadow that enveloped his vision.

Living with blindness was a daily, grueling ordeal, yet my friend met his physical limitations with an irrepressible humor and sharp mental clarity. Rather than retreating into despair, he cultivated a heightened sensory awareness that astonished everyone around him; he could read the water’s current by the gentle tug on his line and sense the weather shifting by the drop in humidity against his skin. At night, he claimed, his mind compensated for the waking void with vivid, technicolor dreams—brilliant visual landscapes that kept his connection to the glowing world alive. 

Through these internal resources, he achieved a quiet triumph over his condition. Fishing was not merely a pastime for him, but a creative act of adaptation. Deprived of physical sight, he summoned deep-seated memories and a rich, active imagination to construct the world around him. He mapped the riverbank, the arc of the fish, and the golden hour light entirely within his mind, finding profound purpose and beauty in the depths of his personal darkness.

Tragically, the resilience that had sustained him for so long could not shield him from a far more devastating physical decline. A cruel illness gradually ravaged his body, stripping away his mobility and forcing him to surrender the fierce independence he had fought so hard to maintain. Watching him lose the ability to hold a fishing rod, walk unassisted, and finally manage his own basic care was agonizing. Before long, his vibrant spirit was swallowed by the relentless decay of his body, culminating in a grim and painful death.

In the wake of his passing, I often find myself returning to the river alone, crushed by a quiet, bitter grief. People often try to romanticize such tragedies, clinging to the comforting idea that inner grace, memory, or artistic beauty can somehow redeem a life ended in agony. But having witnessed the brutal reality of his final days, I find myself rejecting those easy platitudes. Sitting by the cold water, I struggle to believe that any amount of poetic meaning or recalled light can truly soften or justify the unbearable depth of human suffering.

"Ten o’clock," I whispered, standing just half a step behind Arthur on the gravel bar. "Hold it there. Feel the load of the line bending the graphite. Now... cast forward to two."

Arthur’s right arm moved with a fluid, disciplined grace. The fly line hissed through the cool morning air, uncoiling in a high, invisible arc above the river before settling onto the current with barely a ripple. He couldn't see the line, nor the dark, trout-rich eddy where the water curled around a submerged boulder. But he felt it all. He had mapped the world in his mind through sound, memory, and the intricate feedback of tension passed down twenty feet of tapered leader.

"Directly ahead," I told him. "Twelve o’clock. Twelve yards out."

Arthur smiled, his unseeing eyes fixed on the blank horizon of the opposite bank. "I can hear the pocket," he said softly, his voice carrying the deep, easy cadence of a man who had long made peace with his darkness. "The water drops three inches right behind that rock. It hums a slightly lower key."

For two seasons, I had been teaching Arthur the mechanics of fly casting using this system of spatial orientation. We converted the river into the face of a giant clock, using degrees of angle, distance in yards, and the auditory cues of rushing water. But in truth, Arthur was the one teaching me. Blinded six years earlier by a degenerative condition, he had transformed a devastating loss into a profound spiritual awakening. 

He often spoke of his sightlessness not as an absence, but as a different kind of presence. "When you lose your eyes, you stop taking the world for granted," he told me once as we sat on the bank, sipping bitter coffee from a thermos. "You sighted people are distracted by the surface of things—the gloss, the color. But I get to touch the bones of reality. The wind isn't just a view; it's a map. The river isn't just blue; it's a living, breathing pulse."

I admired him immensely. In Arthur, I saw the ultimate triumph of the human spirit—a man who had woven poetry out of misfortune, using philosophy and sensory adaptation to construct a life of quiet dignity and transcendent beauty. I believed, as many romantic souls do, that the depth of a person's character could shield them from the cold brutality of existence.

That belief shattered on a dark, late-autumn evening.

We were fishing a stretch of the river bordered by steep, shale bluffs. A sudden, unseasonable cloudburst upstream had turned the placid water into a roiling, clay-colored torrent in a matter of minutes. As the river rose rapidly, I shouted for Arthur to retreat to higher ground.

I was twenty yards downstream when I heard the sickening sound of crumbling earth. 

Arthur had misjudged the edge of the shelf—a margin of error so tiny it would have meant nothing to a man with sight, who simply would have stepped back. But in the chaotic din of the swollen river, his acute hearing was rendered useless by the deafening roar of water. His spatial clock failed him. The bank collapsed under his boots, dropping him instantly into the freezing, fast-moving deep.

I threw myself toward the bank, screaming his name, but the current was merciless. Because he could not see the branches hanging low over the water, he could not reach for them. Because he could not see the sharp, submerged river rocks, he was slammed brutally into them, entirely defenseless. His adapted senses, so refined in moments of calm, were useless in the blind panic of the flood. I saw his arms flailing, heard a single, strangled cry of sheer terror—unpoetic, unphilosophical, utterly helpless—before he was swept under the dark, churned foam.

They found his body three miles downstream early the next morning, tangled in a strainer of driftwood. 

In the days that followed, the grief was heavy, but the spiritual disorientation was worse. I returned to the riverbank alone, holding Arthur's rod, looking out over the water where we had mapped the world together. 

I realized then the lie I had chosen to believe. I had used Arthur’s resilience as a cozy, comforting metaphor. I had convinced myself that his poetic acceptance of blindness redeemed the tragedy of his sightlessness—that the human mind’s ability to find beauty in suffering somehow neutralized the suffering itself. 

It was a illusion. When the cold, indifferent physics of the world collided with Arthur’s fragile flesh, his spiritual nobility offered him no armor. His blindness had not been a quiet blessing in disguise; it had been a terrible, terrifying deficit that ultimately trapped him in a nightmare of flailing, dark panic.

The river did not care about Arthur’s philosophical grace. The water was just water, cold and heavy, and the rock was just rock. As I watched the river flow past, indifferent to the man it had erased, I was left with a chilling, sobering truth: the emotional artifice and poetic beauty we build around life's hardships are merely fragile blankets thrown over a ruthless reality. Resilience is noble, but it is not a redemption. It cannot save us, and it cannot undo the absolute, uncaring indignities of the world.

When the sun finally dipped beneath the jagged horizon, the valley was swallowed by a deep, impenetrable **darkness**. The familiar landmarks vanished, replaced by shifting shadows and the quiet uncertainty of the night.

We stood shoulder to shoulder at the edge of the overgrown woods. It was easy to feel small in such silence, to let the weight of the unknown test **our** resolve. Yet, looking back was no longer an option; the only direction left was forward.

With a firm grip on the blade, I stepped up to **cut** a path through the tangled brush. Every strike of steel against the stubborn branches echoed into the night, a defiant rhythm against the gloom. With each fallen limb, a little more starlight filtered through the dense canopy, lighting the next few inches of the trail. 

We knew the morning was still hours away, but as long as we kept moving, the shadows had no hold on us. Together, we carved a way through the night, step by fragile step.

counterfactuals.output: His hands were like water-logged oak, calloused and mapped by years of salt, but they could not find the tiny eye of the brass hook in the gathering dusk. I sat beside him in the narrow dory, threading his line with pale, shivering bait and placing the cork grip into his palm. "The water is bruised plum tonight," I told him, and he nodded, casting out into the invisible swell with a whip-crack precision born of pure memory. He read the sea through vibrations—the twitch of the monofilament between his fingertips, the low, hollow thrum of the tide against the cedar hull—while I gave him the rest: the way the gulls hovered like white ash in the wind, the golden grease of the sunset smearing the horizon. For hours, we existed in this quiet commerce, trading my eyes for his patience, pulling silver-scaled things from the deep that he recognized by weight and slime alone. But as the cold set in and the stars pierced the sky like ice needles, he slumped against the gunwale, a sudden, terrible frailty snapping the illusion of his strength. I reached out to steady him, feeling the sharp, fragile lattice of his ribs beneath his oilskin, hearing the wet, gravelly rattle of the sickness we had rowed out here to forget. I kept talking—describing the phosphorescence bleeding green in our wake, the breathtaking, infinite vault of heaven—painting a world so luminous it made my own chest ache. But he only pressed his forehead against his ruined hands, small and shivering against the immense, dark waters. It was there, with the tide pulling us out toward the open ocean, that I learned the bitter limits of my gift: that beauty is only a fragile light shining on the surface of an indifferent void, brilliant and utterly useless, unable to warm his freezing skin, unable to anchor him to the earth, unable to save either of us from the lightless dark waiting beneath the keel.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary vignette featuring dialogue from a blind former fisherman. Include motifs of worms in the dark, sensory distinctions (like a mollusk vs. a whelk), poetic metaphors about sight loss, and repeat the question "Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?"
counterfactuals.output:
The porch of the gutted shack smelled of dried kelp, tar, and the iron tang of old fish hooks. Bram sat on an overturned gutting tub, his gnarled thumbs tracing the lip of a bucket filled with wet sand and writhing, unseen life. Though the sun was setting over the headland, painting the Atlantic in bruised shades of copper and violet, Bram’s world had long since settled into an absolute, velvety hush.

He thrust his hand deep into the damp grit of the bucket, his thick fingers tangling with the cold, muscular loops within. 

"The lugworms know the truth of it," Bram said. His voice was like two beach stones grinding together in the surf. He didn't turn toward the boy sitting on the steps, but his ears twitched at the youth's shifting feet. "Down in the black silt, six fathoms under the tide, the worms chew through the world. They never saw the sky, so they don't mourn it. They spend their lives wriggling through the heavy, wet dark, digesting the dark, turning it into something clean. Blind, soft things, yet they hold the floor of the ocean together."

He withdrew his hand, letting a handful of sand and twisting bait-worms spill back into the tub. He wiped his palm on his oilskins, staring straight ahead with eyes as cloudy and smooth as sea glass.

"Tell me, lad," Bram asked, his brow furrowing as he leaned into the wind. "Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?"

"It’s almost night, Master Bram," the boy offered quietly. "The sun's just a sliver now."

"The sun," Bram snorted, shaking his head. "A noisy, burning thing. People think losing your eyes is like stepping into a room when the lamp goes out. It isn't. It was an anchor dropped over the side of a boat, dragging my sight down through the green shallows, down past the cold gray, until it hit the seabed where light can't press. My eyes didn't shut; the sea just swallowed the lantern."

He reached into a wooden crate at his side and pulled out two shells, holding them out toward the boy. He didn't need to see them; his callous-worn fingertips read the calcium like script.

"Here," Bram commanded. "Take them. Feel the difference, so you aren't just a boy who looks, but a man who knows."

The boy took the shells, turning them over in his small, smooth palms. 

"That one in your left—that’s a common mollusk," Bram said, his thumb flicking in the air toward the boy's left hand. "A bivalve. Soft, timid thing. It hides behind two smooth, hinged iron doors, dreaming of nothing but plankton, waiting for the sea to feed it. It’s flat, dull, passive."

Bram tapped the shell in the boy’s right hand. "But that—that’s a dog-whelk. Feel the architecture of it. A spiral of heavy armor, ribbed and pitted by the salt. A whelk doesn't wait; it crawls. It bores a hole right through the hard house of a mollusk and eats it alive. You can feel the violence in the whorl of its spine, can't you? A mollusk is just a stone that breathes; a whelk is a horn sounded at the bottom of the bay."

The boy ran his thumb over the sharp, spiraled ridge of the whelk, nodding silently before remembering Bram couldn't see the gesture. "I feel it," he said. "It’s cold. Rough."

"Cold is just the truth stripped of the sun's lies," Bram murmured. 

The wind shifted, carrying the sharp, sweet smell of coming rain and the distant, rhythmic boom of the swell against the granite cliffs. Bram lifted his chin, drinking in the damp air. The vast, quiet dark around him felt deep, fragile, and immense—a quiet sanctuary where the ghosts of red sunsets and blinding sea-glare could no longer scald his head.

He reached out, his hand hovering until it found the bucket of worms again, his fingers plunging back down into the cool, churning soil. 

"The stars will be coming out soon, I suppose," Bram whispered to the darkening air, his voice tinged with a strange, protective dread. "Fierce little pricks of fire, burning up the quiet. Darkness is precious, how long will darkness last?"

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a day on the water between two friends, one of whom has gone blind. Make the dialogue philosophical, melancholic, and deeply sensory, contrasting the companion's clever humor with his tragic, unvarnished decline.
counterfactuals.output:
The wooden skiff groaned as it settled into the black, unbothered glass of the lake. The smell hit them first—a sharp, damp mixture of rotting cedar, cold mud, and the metallic tang of late-September ozone. 

Samuel settled into the middle bench, his hands calloused and familiar against the oars. Across from him sat Julian.

A year ago, Julian’s eyes had been a piercing, restless gray. Now, they were clouded over, milky and unfocused, staring permanently at a horizon six inches in front of his nose. But his posture remained stubbornly upright, despite the harrowing thinness of his frame. His collarbones stood out like dry branches beneath his wool sweater, and his wrists, resting on his knees, trembled with a fine, persistent palsy.

"Well," Julian said, his voice a dry rasp that rasped like fine sandpaper. "Describe the grand expanse, Sam. Tell me the sky is blue so I can pretend to care."

"It’s grey," Samuel said, dipping the oars. The water clapped softly against the cedar hull. *Slap. Swish.* "Thick clouds. The pines on the far shore look like rusted iron."

Julian tilted his head, listening to the drip of water from the raised blades. He reached down, plunging a gaunt, spotted hand into the lake. He winced at the cold, but left his fingers submerged, dragging them through the heavy element.

"It feels like melted ice and dead leaves," Julian murmured. "Sensory poetry. You always did rely too much on the sun, Sam. Sight is a lazy sense. It lets you believe things are solid just because they bounce light back at you. Water doesn't lie. It’s cold, it’s indifferent, and it’s entirely ready to drown us."

"You’re a ray of sunshine, Julian."

"I am a philosopher of the tactile," Julian countered, a sudden, wicked grin flashing across his gaunt face, revealing teeth that seemed too large now that his cheeks had hollowed out. "And as your senior philosopher, I command you to row toward the deep end. If we capsize, at least let it be an event of depth. I’d hate to end up half-buried in shallow mud like an abandoned boot."

Samuel smiled faintly, but the warmth died quickly in his chest. He watched Julian try to pull his hand back into the boat. The effort was absurdly grand; Julian’s forearm shook, muscles knotting under translucent skin, until Samuel reached out and gently hauled his friend's wrist over the gunwale. Julian’s skin was ice-cold, paper-thin, and damp.

Julian didn't pull away, but his smile turned bitter. "Ah. The heavy lift of a dying man's arm. Magnificent. I should charge you for the physical therapy."

"Shut up, Julian."

"No, really. It’s the ultimate irony, isn't it?" Julian leaned his head back, catching the pale, heatless sunlight on his hollow throat. "My mind is as sharp as a freshly honed razor, Sam, yet I am trapped in a meat-suit that is quietly dissolving into broth. I’m a ghost who hasn’t had the good manners to stop breathing."

"You're still here," Samuel said quietly.

"A technicality," Julian replied. He fumbled in his pocket, his trembling fingers searching for his brass lighter and a cigarette. Samuel watched him struggle—the pathetic, unvarnished indignity of a man who used to dismantle arguments at dinner tables with a flick of his wrist, now unable to locate a hinge.

Samuel reached out, took the lighter, clicked it, and held the flame in front of Julian’s face.

Julian paused, smelling the butane. He leaned forward, found the flame with the tip of his paper-wrapped tobacco, and inhaled. A plume of blue-grey smoke drifted into the crisp air, smelling of rich Virginia leaf and impending autumn.

"Thank you," Julian whispered. The cleverness dropped away for a fraction of a second, revealing a vast, terrifying exhaustion. "Is the sun down yet?"

"Not yet. An hour, maybe."

"Good. The dark is horribly redundant for me, but I like the temperature drop. It feels like the world is shrinking to fit my circumference." Julian blew another ring of smoke into the void. "Do you know what I miss most, Sam? Not color. Color is just light throwing a tantrum. I miss the geometry of things. The sharp edge where a roof meets the sky. The horizon cutting the chaos in half."

"The horizon is right behind you," Samuel said, his voice thick. "It’s very sharp today."

Julian chuckled, a wet, rattling sound in his chest that took several seconds to clear. He spat over the side of the boat, the white phlegm disappearing into the black water. "You’re a terrible painter, Sam. You paint with sympathy, which ruins the edges."

He reached out blindly, his hand hovering until it touched the wooden gunwale. His fingers traced the grain, feeling the old coat of varnish, the deep gouges where anchor lines had worn down the wood over decades.

"We used to think we were the ones moving through time," Julian said softly, his voice dropping into the quiet rhythm of the lake. "When we were twenty, sitting on this same water, drinking cheap gin. We thought we were sailing forward. But time is the water, Sam. We are just sitting in a leaky boat, waiting for the wood to rot through."

"Julian..."

"Don't," Julian snapped, though there was no heat in it. Just the hollow echo of a man who had already argued with God and lost. "Don't offer me the comfort of metaphors. My eyes didn't fail because of a grand tragedy; they failed because a few tiny blood vessels decided to burst like cheap pipes. There is no poetry in decay, Sam. Only the smell of damp wool and the fact that I can't see your face."

He paused, his blind, milky eyes fixed on the empty space between them. 

"Is your hair gray yet?" Julian asked, his voice suddenly small, stripped of its intellect, painfully human.

"A bit," Samuel lied. It was almost entirely white.

"Liar," Julian murmured, a faint, ghost-like smile returning to his lips. "You always were a terrible liar."

Samuel pulled on the oars. The wood creaked—a slow, rhythmic heartbeat on the vast, silent water. The shore was drifting further away, disappearing into the twilight fog. 

Julian leaned over the side again, listening to the hiss of the water parting against the bow. He closed his eyes—a pointless gesture, but an ancient habit—and let the cold spray wet his sunken cheeks.

"Row a little faster, Sam," the blind man whispered into the gather of the dark. "Before the lake realizes we're here."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a story centered on the theme that "the power of beauty to right all wrongs is hard to sell," using the bond between a guide and a blind fisherman to explore darkness, memory, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
The river at dusk smelled of cold iron, wet hemlock, and the sharp, metallic tang of coming frost. 

Jonah rested the oars in their locks, letting the drift-boat settle into the glass-still eddy near the mouth of the canyon. Across the thrumming current, the late October sun was bleeding out against the jagged granite cliffs, painting the water in stripes of violet, bruised orange, and spun gold.

"It’s a cathedral today, Elias," Jonah said softly, his voice barely rising above the murmur of the river. "The light is hitting the high wall just right. Looks like the stone is glowing from the inside. Like the whole world is being forgiven for something."

In the bow of the boat, Elias sat motionless. He wore a faded canvas jacket, stiff with years of salt and river mud. Dark, unblinking eyes stared out beneath the brim of a battered oilskin hat, seeing nothing. He had lost his sight twelve years ago, when an exploding boiler on a deep-sea trawler took his optics and, in the same fiery breath, swept his seven-year-old daughter, Clara, off the deck into the grey abyss of the Bering Strait.

Elias unspooled a few feet of line through his gnarled fingers. He didn't use a fly rod anymore; he used a handline, feeling the river through the vibration of monofilament wrapped around his thumb. 

"Forgiven for what?" Elias asked. His voice was like two river stones grinding together.

"I don't know," Jonah replied, leaning forward on his knees. Jonah was twenty-four, hired by Elias’s sister to keep the old man from drowning himself under the guise of 'guiding.' Jonah believed fervently in the redemptive arc of nature. He believed that if he could just describe the world vividly enough, if he could project enough radiance into the void behind Elias’s eyes, the darkness would loosen its grip. "Just... everything. The tragedy of things. You look at a canyon like this, under a sky like this, and it feels like the beauty of it makes up for the rest. Like it balances the ledger."

Elias gave a quiet, humorless grunt. He flicked his wrist, sending a weighted hook and a bit of yarn into the dark seam between two currents. "That's a young man's math, Jonah. Beauty don't pay debts."

"It has weight, though," Jonah insisted, watching a bald eagle slice across the illuminated sky. "It has to count for something."

"It counts for the people who can afford to look at it," Elias said. He closed his eyes—a habit of muscle memory, though it made no difference—and settled into the rhythm of the water. 

In the dark, Elias did not see the golden cliff or the eagle. He felt the cold air pooling in the hollow of his collarbone. He smelled the pine needle rot. And, as always, memory filled the empty space where the world used to be. Memory was not a gift to Elias; it was a haunt. 

He remembered the exact blue of Clara’s rubber boots. He remembered the blinding white flash of the boiler rupture, followed by the infinite, absolute black that had never lifted. People often told him how lucky he was to have lived, how resilient he was to keep fishing. They told him the river was beautiful, that the mountains were timeless, as if the landscape were a poultice he could press against his ruined life to draw out the grief.

They were trying to sell him a bill of goods. They wanted him to accept that a nice sunset was fair trade for a buried child and a dark world. 

"You've got a bite," Jonah whispered suddenly. "Two feet left of the eddy. Something big."

Elias felt it a fraction of a second before Jonah spoke—a subtle, heavy dead-weight on the line, followed by three sharp, rhythmic thumps. The strike of a winter steelhead, a fish that had traveled hundreds of miles through sea and dark river to return to its birthplace.

Elias set the hook with a sharp jerk of his arm. 

The river erupted. Even without sight, Elias felt the violence of it. The line hummed, vibrating through the bones of his forearm like a plucked harp string. The fish tore downstream, ripping line from the spool at Elias's feet. 

"He's jumping!" Jonah yelled, standing up, the oars clicking in their sockets. "My God, Elias! He’s huge! Three feet out of the water—the sun is catching the spray, it looks like shattered glass! The side of him is crimson—pure crimson!"

Jonah was breathing hard, his voice thick with a genuine, desperate wonder. He wanted this for Elias. He wanted the magnificent, shining reality of this creature to pierce the old man's gloom. He was trying, with all his young heart, to sell the light.

"Keep the bow straight," Elias commanded, his posture rigid, his hands working the line with cold, practiced precision. He didn't care about the shattered glass spray. He didn't care about the crimson stripe. 

He cared about the weight. He felt the fish’s desperate, furious desire to live, translated down thirty feet of nylon. He felt its heart hammering against the current. It was fighting the invisible pull, just as he had fought the smoke and the freezing water twelve years ago, grasping at nothing, coming up empty.

For ten minutes, the battle raged in the dark space between the boat and the riverbed. Slowly, inch by inch, Elias dragged the creature out of its wild element toward the wooden gunwale.

"He's right here," Jonah breathed, reaching down with the rubber net. "Elias, look—I mean, feel this. You have to touch him."

Jonah scooped the net, lifting the fish partially out of the water, resting its heavy belly against the side of the boat.

"Touch him," Jonah urged softly. "He’s magnificent. Tell me that isn't something sacred."

Elias hesitated. Then, he reached down into the freezing water. His calloused fingers slid over the cool, muscular flank of the steelhead. He felt the slime layer, the fine armor of scales, the frantic, rib-rattling gasps of the gills. He felt the sheer, breathtaking perfection of the animal—a masterpiece forged by miles of cold water and instinct.

It was, objectively, a marvel. A thing of profound, undeniable beauty.

Elias pulled his hand back as if he had touched hot iron.

"What is it?" Jonah asked, the excitement fading from his voice, replaced by a sudden, hollow dread.

Elias wiped his wet hand on his canvas trousers. The cold water dripped from his knuckles.

"It’s just a fish trying not to die," Elias said softly. "And it’s going to die anyway. Maybe today, maybe next year in some shallow creek."

"Elias..." Jonah’s voice cracked. "It’s beautiful. Doesn't it... doesn't it make you feel anything?"

Elias leaned back in the bow, facing the direction where he knew the sun was setting, though the warmth had already retreated behind the mountains, leaving only the biting cold.

"It makes me angry," Elias said. The fury in his voice was not hot; it was cold and ancient, smoothed round by years of tide. "You keep trying to show me the world, Jonah. You tell me about the light, the eagles, the colors on the fish. You think if you describe enough pretty things, it’ll make the darkness make sense. You think beauty is a cure."

Jonah sat down slowly on the rower’s bench. The river gently rocked the boat. "I just thought... if you could remember what it looks like..."

"I remember," Elias interrupted. "That’s the curse of it. I remember the exact shade of the sky the morning I lost her. It was a clear, crisp day. Beautiful. The sun came up over the ocean like a golden coin, and it didn't do a damn thing to save my girl. It just kept shining while she sank."

Elias reached down, found the leader, and pulled the hook gently from the steelhead’s jaw. With a heavy splash, the fish kicked its tail and vanished back into the black depths of the canyon water.

"Beauty doesn't care about us, Jonah," Elias said, his voice dropping to a harsh whisper. "It doesn't balance anything. It just sits there, looking pretty, while the world breaks you in half. To offer a sunset to a grieving man... it’s like offering a starving man a painting of a feast. It’s a hard sell, kid. And I’m not buying."

Silence settled over the boat, thick and suffocating. The canyon swallowed the last of the ambient light. The violet cliffs turned to charcoal, then to absolute, impenetrable black.

Jonah looked at his hands on the oars. For the first time since he had taken the job, he felt the true weight of the dark. He had believed that sight was a bridge he could build for Elias. He realized now that he was standing on one side of a chasm, waving a lantern, completely ignorant of how deep the crevasse actually was.

He couldn't fix it. The river couldn't fix it. The mountains were just rock; the light was just radiation hitting dust. None of it had a heart.

Jonah took a slow breath. He stopped trying to see for Elias. He closed his eyes.

The wind rustled the dead leaves in the alders along the bank. The river hissed against the wooden hull. The air smelled of frost and old water.

"It's getting cold," Jonah said quietly. No flourishes. No descriptions of the stars that were beginning to pierce the dark velvet above them. Just the truth.

Elias shifted in the bow. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small piece of dried deer meat, chewing it slowly. 

"Yeah," Elias said. "The temperature drops fast once the sun goes down over the ridge."

"Should I row us back?"

"Not yet," Elias said. He lowered his hand back over the gunwale, trailing his fingers in the rushing, invisible water. He didn't ask what the sky looked like. He didn't ask if the stars were out. 

Instead, he listened to the steady, rhythmic oarsman’s breath beside him, and the endless, indifferent march of the river taking everything down to the sea.

Jonah sat in the dark with him. He didn't offer a light. He didn't try to sell the night. He just sat there, cold and quiet, letting the darkness be dark, and for the first time, Elias didn't feel quite so entirely alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a haunting piece of poetic prose about a blind man who learns to navigate fishing by sound and memory, incorporating vivid imagery about light-sensitive bait, dreamscapes, and the smell of old books.
counterfactuals.output:
The dark was not an absence of light, but a cathedral of echoes. 

Long after the white fog settled permanently behind his eyelids, Arthur learned that the lake spoke in consonants. The sharp *tock* of a water beetle against cedar; the low, resonant thrum of deep water pressing against the skiff’s hull; the thin, weeping sibilance of wind through the reed beds. He navigated by these sonorities, mapping the unseen topography of the bay with a fisherman’s dark echolocation. His oars dipped without a splash, rising only to drop beads of water that struck the surface like steady, miniature bells. Memory filled the voids: he remembered where the drowned willow leaned, where the shelf of limestone dropped into the icy, sunless throat of the channel.

In his lap rested the tin tackle box. When he pried open its rusted latch, a ghost exhaled into the night air—a scent so thick and incongruous it made his chest ache. It smelled of old books. Not merely wet paper, but the heavy, velvet aroma of an ancient archive: decaying lignin, dry leather bindings, foxed margins, and the sweet, dusty vanilla of slowly crumbling centuries. Touch by touch, he sorted through the trays of his memory, his calloused fingertips brushing past lead sinkers and silver spoons until they found the small, airtight glass vial.

Inside slept the bait. They were strange, deep-trench larvae—light-sensitive, chemiluminescent soft bodies that starved for the dark. The moment Arthur pulled the glass stopper, exposing them to the nocturnal air, they began to bleed their cold, violent blue light. Arthur could not see the eerie radiance that turned his knuckles into translucent alabaster, but he felt it: a faint, prickling vibration on his skin, a micro-warmth like a fevered pulse. 

He threaded the glowing creature onto the hook by touch alone, feeling the soft tremor of its dying bioluminescence against his thumb. He swung the rod back. The line whistled—a high, sharp needle piercing the quiet—and the baited hook plunged into the black depth. 

He waited.

Sleep was a shallow tide that pulled him under into sudden, vivid dreamscapes. In these sleeping visions, he was not blind, nor was he above the surface. He swam through a drowned library submerged beneath forty feet of black water. Endless rows of waterlogged folios swayed like giant kelp; pale, blind fish with translucent ribs drifted between the floating, ink-drifted pages. The light-sensitive bait trailed from his hand like a burning star, illuminating forgotten words that rose from the parchment in streams of iridescent bubbles.

A sudden, sharp tug shattered the glass of his sleep.

The line went taut, humming like a plucked cello string. The vibration traveled up the graphite rod, through his palm, and straight into the marrow of his collarbone. Deep below, something ancient and heavy had swallowed the dying light. 

Arthur did not reel it in immediately. He sat in the dark, hand vibrating with the furious, unseen pulse of the creature in the abyss. He leaned close to the water, listening to the frantic *slap-slap* of the tail against the submerged thermocline, inhaling the cold, mossy breath of the lake that smelled, so impossibly, of turning pages. He held the line gently, feeling the exact moment the fish gave up its fight, caught in the dark between his memory of the sun and the creature's thirst for the fire it could never comprehend.
